How drift is judged

Method, as implemented in drift_detection.py + drift_adaptation.py

Two different detectors watch the same forecast-error stream live. ADWIN keeps an adaptive window over the errors and fires when two sub-windows disagree beyond its bound; Page-Hinkley accumulates deviations from the running mean and fires when the cumulative sum crosses its threshold. Either detector firing is logged as a control event with its reason — those events are what this page counts, so a firing here is a firing the controller actually recorded, not a recomputation.

A separate windowed monitor pairs each forecast with the value observed one horizon later and compares the window RMSE against the baseline RMSE read from the saved model artifact. Drift is declared only after consecutive drifting windows, so one bad minute cannot trigger it. When it declares drift, it writes a recalibration artifact — an empirical residual radius recomputed from the observed pairs — and nothing else changes: the live model is never swapped automatically.

The campaign check on this page is independent of both detectors: every recorded predictive-ml prediction is paired with the telemetry value exactly 5 s later on the same link, the pooled error stream is split in half, and first-half vs second-half RMSE/MAE is the comparison. Flat halves mean the forecaster aged evenly over the campaign; a growing second half is what real drift would look like in this data.
